 Coinone Vendor Breach May Expose 11 Data Types
 Daniel Roth 
 Updated Nov 15, 2026 · 17 min read 
 Photo: MART PRODUCTION / Pexels 
 South Korean crypto exchange Coinone told customers on November 15, 2026 that an outside attacker broke into the servers of its customer-support contractor, and Chosun reported that the intrusion exposed customer data held by that vendor. The Coinone data breach did not touch the exchange’s own systems, according to the company. It hit MetaM, the firm that handles customer consultations on Coinone’s behalf.

 The list of data that may have leaked is long and sensitive. It runs from names and email addresses to passwords, resident registration numbers and crypto wallet addresses. Cointelegraph covered the exchange’s warning that affected users should expect phishing and identity-theft attempts. Coinone has not said how many people are affected.
 This analysis walks through what the notice confirms, what it leaves open, and why a support-desk leak can hurt more than its label suggests. It also looks at how the incident fits a pattern we have tracked all year, including the CSCTelecom SMS leak that exposed 125M+ messages , where a service provider rather than the brand itself held the exposed data. Everything below sticks to what Coinone and named outlets have stated. Where the record is silent, we say so.

 Add now Coinone Data Breach: What the November 15 Notice Confirms
 Coinone’s public notice is short on numbers but clear on the mechanism. In the company’s own words, “An external attacker made an unauthorized intrusion into the servers of MetaM, a commissioned service provider handling customer support, resulting in the leakage of customer personal information.” That sentence sets the frame for everything else. The attacker went after a contractor, and the contractor held records that customers had handed over while asking for help.
 The exposed material is data customers supplied during customer-support consultations. That detail matters because it explains why the damage varies from person to person. A customer who asked a simple question about fees may have shared little. A customer who had trouble logging in, or who needed an identity check, may have shared far more. Coinone said as much, noting that the affected data differs by customer.

 Customers who never contacted the support center were reported as unaffected. For an exchange with a large user base, that carve-out could shrink the exposed group considerably, though the company has not published a headcount to prove it. Until it does, the size of the affected pool remains an open question and any figure circulating online should be treated as unverified.
 Several Korean and international outlets carried the story on the day of the notice. SBS framed it as customer personal information leaked through a third-party vendor hack, while The Herald Business described a hack of an outsourced call-center operator. The framing is consistent across outlets, and none of them has reported a breach of Coinone’s own databases.
 The 11 Data Types That May Be Exposed
 The notice lists eleven categories of information that may have been exposed. Coinone did not claim that every category leaked for every customer. It described the list as the full range of what could appear in support records, depending on what each person shared.
 Data category Why it matters Main abuse risk 
 Name Anchors every other data point to a real person Targeted phishing 
 Phone number Direct line to the customer Voice phishing, SMS scams 
 Email address Common login and recovery handle Fake Coinone emails, account recovery attempts 
 Date of birth Used in identity checks Identity verification fraud 
 Bank-account number Links the person to a funding source Impersonation of the exchange or bank 
 Password Opens accounts, especially if reused Credential stuffing on other services 
 Resident registration number National ID number used across Korean services Identity theft 
 ID-document issue date Secondary identity check field Passing knowledge-based verification 
 Home address Physical location of the customer Mail fraud, doxxing, social engineering 
 Wallet address Public view of on-chain holdings Targeting of high-balance holders 
 Transaction ID (TXID) Proves a specific transfer happened Convincing fake support scripts 
 The risk column reflects our analysis of how each field is typically abused. It is not a list of confirmed incidents. No outlet has reported any of these abuse cases tied to this leak so far.
 Alone, most of these fields are low value. Together they are a ready-made kit. A scammer who holds a name, a phone number, a bank account and a TXID can open a call by describing a real transfer the victim made. That level of detail beats most people’s skepticism, and it is the reason security teams treat support transcripts as high-risk data.
 Why Support Records Are a Goldmine for Attackers
 Customer-support systems collect exactly what security policies tell staff not to collect. People paste screenshots into chats. They read out account numbers over the phone. They type a password to prove they own the account, even when the agent never asked. A support archive becomes a long, messy file of everything a customer should have kept private.
 That is the heart of this incident. Coinone’s trading engine, wallet infrastructure and member database sit behind controls built for financial risk. A support vendor’s ticketing or call-recording stack usually sits behind lighter ones. Attackers know the gap exists, and they pick the softer door when the main entrance is hardened.
 The advice Coinone gave on passwords hints at the scale of the problem. The exchange told customers who shared a password during support to change it, and to change any reused copy on other sites. Nobody should send a password to a support agent, and exchanges generally tell users so. Yet the notice implies that some customers did, and that those words now sit in a vendor’s records.
 Support data also ages badly. A trading log from 2023 may mean little today. A resident registration number, a home address and a date of birth stay valid for years. A single leak can feed fraud campaigns long after the news cycle moves on, which is why regulators and security teams treat identity data as a permanent exposure rather than a one-time event.
 What Stayed Separate: Accounts, Trading and Wallets
 Coinone said its member-account, trading and virtual-asset wallet systems run separately from MetaM’s servers. The company reported no evidence of a direct compromise of those systems. For customers holding assets on the exchange, that is the most important line in the notice.
 It does not mean the assets are risk-free. Separation protects the systems, but it does not protect the people if an attacker can talk their way in. A criminal armed with a customer’s support history might try to reset credentials, pass a phone verification or trick the customer into approving a withdrawal. The vendor breach turns a technical problem into a social-engineering problem.
 The contrast with a core-infrastructure compromise is sharp. Our explainer on the Binance $6.34B hack and the EIP-7702 sweep covers a case where the signing layer itself was the target. Nothing reported about Coinone suggests anything like that. No outlet has reported stolen crypto or unauthorized movement of Coinone’s assets.
 One point deserves care. The phrase no evidence of a direct compromise is a statement about what the investigation has found so far. It is not a guarantee about what a longer forensic review will show. Readers should expect Coinone to update the notice if its findings change.
 What Remains Unconfirmed
 Breach coverage tends to blur confirmed facts and plausible guesses. With the Coinone case, the gap between the two is wide, so it helps to separate them.
 Claim Status Basis 
 Attacker accessed MetaM’s servers Confirmed Coinone’s November 15 notice 
 Data came from customer-support consultations Confirmed Coinone’s notice and press reports 
 Coinone account, trading and wallet systems separate from MetaM Confirmed by Coinone Company statement, no evidence of direct compromise 
 Customers who never contacted support are unaffected Reported Coinone’s statement as relayed by press 
 Exact number of affected customers or records Unconfirmed No figure published 
 Every data category exposed for every customer Unconfirmed Exposure varies by customer 
 Theft or unauthorized movement of crypto Unconfirmed No reports of loss 
 The first gap is the headcount. Without a number, nobody can judge whether this is a small leak among heavy support users or a broad one. Outlets such as Aju Press have reported the incident as an external contractor hack, but none has put a figure on the victims.
 The second gap is attribution. Coinone calls the intruder an external attacker and says nothing more. We do not know if the attacker was a criminal group, a lone actor or something else. We also do not know how the intruder got in, how long they stayed or whether the data has been posted for sale. Those details usually emerge later, if at all.
 The third gap is timing of harm. A leak announced today may have started days or weeks earlier. Coinone’s notice gives a public disclosure date but, in the fact record we can verify, no full timeline. Readers who contacted support at any point in recent months should act as if they could be on the list.
 Phishing Is the Real Near-Term Risk
 The first wave of damage from a leak like this rarely involves a hacker draining a vault. It involves a message on a phone. Coinone itself warned customers about phishing and identity theft, as Cointelegraph’s coverage made clear, and the warning fits the data. Names, phone numbers and email addresses are the raw material for convincing scams.
 Consider how a scam might look. A text arrives that claims to come from Coinone. It mentions a real transaction ID, or a real bank account ending, and urges the recipient to confirm their identity through a link. The link leads to a clone of the exchange login page. A person who has just read news about the leak might spot the trick. A person who has not may hand over credentials and two-factor codes in under a minute.
 Voice scams carry an added edge. A caller who knows a customer’s birth date and bank account sounds legitimate. The breach gives scammers a script. They no longer need to guess who holds an account at the exchange, because the leaked records tell them.
 The defensive rule is simple. Treat any unsolicited contact that mentions Coinone as hostile until you verify it through the official app or website, typed in by hand. No legitimate support agent needs your password or one-time codes, and nobody should read them aloud to a caller.
 Resident Registration Numbers Raise the Stakes
 The most worrying item on the list is the resident registration number. South Korea uses this number across banking, telecom, healthcare and government services. Unlike a password, a person cannot swap it for a new one at will. Once it is in criminal hands, it can stay there for life.

 Pair it with a name, a birth date and an ID-document issue date, and an attacker holds most of what many identity checks ask for. That combination can support attempts to open accounts, take out loans or hijack phone numbers. The fact sheet does not say that any of this has happened, and the notice says the data present varies by customer. Still, anyone who shared ID details with a support agent should assume the risk is real.
 This is where the support-channel design matters. Exchanges collect identity details for verification, so the data has to flow somewhere. The question regulators will ask is whether it should sit in a vendor’s tooling at all, and for how long.
 Customers in this position should check whether their phone carrier and banks offer alerts or locks on new accounts opened in their name. We cannot list specific tools here without verified sources, so use the official channels of your own providers rather than links sent in messages.
 The Third-Party Vendor Problem
 Outsourcing support is standard practice. It cuts cost, adds multilingual coverage and lets a company scale during busy periods. It also creates a second security perimeter that the company does not fully control. The Coinone incident shows what happens when that perimeter fails.
 A pattern runs through recent breaches that began at a supplier or partner. When we covered the Amicus Lex leak that affected 20,028 people , the story centered on a service holding sensitive records for a customer base far larger than its own security staff. The Fireworks AI breaches, two in 18 days , reached chat transcripts stored on a vendor platform. The details differ, but the lesson repeats. Data held by a partner is only as safe as the partner’s weakest control.
 The company that collects the data stays accountable to its customers, no matter who ran the servers. Coinone’s notice reflects that reality. It describes MetaM as a commissioned service provider and still takes responsibility for the notification and the advice that follows. Regulators in most jurisdictions take the same view.
 Good vendor management covers four things. It limits what the vendor can see, so agents never handle full ID numbers. It sets short retention periods so old transcripts disappear. It demands logging and alerting at the vendor, and it tests the vendor’s defenses the way it tests its own. Companies that skip these steps pay later, in notifications, investigations and lost trust.
 How the Coinone Incident Compares With Other Recent Leaks
 Placing the breach beside other incidents we have covered helps size it. The table below uses only details from our earlier reporting and the Coinone notice. It does not rank severity, because the Coinone victim count is unknown.
 Incident Where the data sat Reported scale Core systems hit? 
 Coinone and MetaM Support vendor servers Not disclosed No evidence reported 
 Amicus Lex leak Legal-tech service 20,028 people Service itself breached 
 CSCTelecom SMS leak Messaging provider 125M+ SMS Provider’s own data exposed 
 Fireworks AI breaches AI platform and chat transcripts 2 breaches in 18 days Platform breached 
 Binance EIP-7702 sweep Signing and wallet layer $6.34B in our headline Yes, core custody path 
 Coinone sits at the milder end on one axis. The company reports no hit on core systems, and no loss of funds has been reported. It sits at the harsher end on another. Identity data, not cryptography, is what leaked, and identity data cannot be rotated like a key.
 That mix explains why the story drew coverage across so many outlets, including Chosun, SBS, The Herald Business, Aju Press and Cointelegraph, within hours of the notice. A breach with no stolen coins is less dramatic than a hack. It can still do more lasting harm to the people involved.
 What Coinone Customers Should Do Now
 Coinone’s own advice is narrow. It tells customers who shared passwords during support to change their Coinone passwords and any reused passwords elsewhere. Our recommendations go a step further, based on standard practice for a leak involving identity and contact data.

 If you shared a password in a support chat or call
 Change the Coinone password first, then every other account that used the same one. Use a password manager to create unique passwords. Turn on two-factor authentication with an authenticator app rather than SMS, since your phone number may now sit in an attacker’s hands.
 If you shared ID details or bank information
 Watch your bank statements and your credit and telecom records for activity you did not start. Contact your bank through its official number if anything looks wrong. Consider asking your carrier about added protection against SIM swaps and unauthorized line changes.
 If you never contacted support
 Coinone reports that you are unaffected. Still, scammers often spray messages at whole user lists, so apply the same caution to unexpected messages. Use the official app, and never follow links in texts or emails about your account.
 Your situation Priority action Follow-up 
 Shared a password with support Change Coinone and reused passwords Enable app-based two-factor authentication 
 Shared ID or bank details Monitor accounts and statements Ask bank and carrier about added protections 
 Shared wallet address or TXID only Expect targeted scam messages Verify any contact through the official app 
 Never contacted support Stay alert to phishing No known exposure reported by Coinone 
 What Exchanges and Vendors Should Change
 For exchanges, the lesson is to treat the support desk as part of the attack surface. Agents should never need a customer’s password, and tooling should block it. A chat system can flag and mask strings that look like credentials, account numbers or national ID numbers before they reach storage. That single control would have shrunk the data at risk in a case like this.
 Verification should move away from reading secrets aloud. Many exchanges now use in-app prompts to confirm identity, so the agent sees a yes or no result rather than the underlying numbers. The fewer secrets that pass through a human channel, the less a vendor breach can reveal.
 Vendors need monitoring that matches the sensitivity of the data they hold. A detection service that watches for unusual access can cut the time an intruder stays inside. Our primer on managed detection and response explains how that kind of service works and what it can and cannot catch. For a call-center contractor, round-the-clock monitoring is a reasonable contract requirement, not a luxury.
 Retention also deserves a hard look. Keeping transcripts for years raises the payoff for attackers and adds little value to customers. Short, documented retention windows, with automatic deletion, turn a future breach into a smaller one. For more reading on defensive practice, see our security coverage hub .
 Market and Regulatory Impact
 No outlet we reviewed reported a price move, a withdrawal spike or a trading halt tied to the Coinone notice. We will not guess at one. The breach touched support data rather than custody, and markets tend to react more to stolen funds than to leaked contact details.
 The more likely impact is on trust and compliance. Exchanges compete on security reputation, and a support-vendor failure invites customers to ask how their data is handled across the whole chain. Rival platforms will face the same questions, and some will review their own contractors this week.
 On the regulatory side, we cannot cite new measures. The fresh reports we reviewed did not provide verified 2025 or 2026 enforcement details for other Korean exchanges, and they did not describe specific new rules tied to this case. What we can say is that data-protection regimes in most jurisdictions require notification, cooperation with authorities and safeguards over outsourced processing. How Korean regulators apply those duties here will become clear only as they respond.
 For Coinone, the near-term cost is operational. The company has to field customer questions, support affected users and complete its forensic work, all while its main support channel is under a cloud. The longer-term cost depends on whether the victim count turns out to be small or large, and whether any fraud traces back to this leak.
 Five Predictions for the Weeks Ahead
 These are our judgments based on how similar incidents have unfolded. They are not facts and carry no confirmed dates.
 Coinone will publish more detail. Pressure from customers and media usually forces a follow-up with a timeline, a clearer scope and possibly a victim count.
 Phishing reports will rise. Scam messages that mention Coinone are likely to circulate, and the exchange will probably issue repeat warnings.
 Rival exchanges will audit their support vendors. Expect quiet contract reviews and public reassurances about data handling at competing platforms.
 Support data will get masked by default. More firms will adopt tools that strip passwords and ID numbers from transcripts before storage.
 Oversight of outsourced processing will tighten. Regulators often respond to vendor breaches with guidance on contractor controls, though timing and form remain uncertain.
 The takeaway: a leak from a support contractor can do real harm without a single coin leaving a wallet. Customers should act on the password advice now, and the industry should treat the help desk as a critical system.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 What happened in the Coinone data breach?
 An external attacker gained unauthorized access to the servers of MetaM, the company that handles customer support for Coinone. The attacker accessed or extracted data that customers supplied during support consultations. Coinone announced the incident on November 15, 2026.
 Was my crypto stolen?
 No theft has been reported. Coinone says its member-account, trading and wallet systems are separate from MetaM’s servers and that it has no evidence of a direct compromise of them. Any claim of stolen funds linked to this breach is unconfirmed.
 What personal data may have leaked?
 The notice lists names, phone numbers, email addresses, dates of birth, bank-account numbers, passwords, resident registration numbers, ID-document issue dates, home addresses, wallet addresses and transaction IDs. Not every customer had every item exposed, since the data depends on what each person shared with support.
 How do I know if I am affected?
 Customers who never contacted the support center were reported as unaffected. If you spoke or chatted with support, assume some of your details may be involved, and follow the password and phishing advice above. Coinone has not published a way to check individual exposure in the reports we reviewed.
 Should I change my password?
 Yes, if you ever shared a password during support. Coinone told such customers to change their Coinone passwords and any reused passwords on other services. Even if you did not share one, switching to a unique password and app-based two-factor authentication is cheap insurance.
 How many customers are affected?
 Unknown. Coinone has not disclosed the number of affected customers or records, and no outlet has published a verified figure. Treat any number you see online as unconfirmed until the company states one.
 How can I spot a Coinone phishing message?
 Be suspicious of any text, email or call that mentions Coinone, especially one that cites a real transaction or bank detail and asks you to click a link or share a code. Open the official app or type the address yourself instead. Never read out passwords or one-time codes to a caller.
